claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and compressive strength in its single-phase solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has high plasticity.
As-cast single-phase CoCrFeNiTi has moderate lattice distortion and no significant nanoscale precipitates.
Insufficient nanoscale precipitation and lattice distortion govern the relatively low hardness and strength of single-phase CoCrFeNiTi.
A low obstacle density permits relatively facile dislocation motion in the initial alloy.
Facile dislocation motion produces lower hardness and strength but higher plasticity in the initial alloy.
A controlled heat treatment or minor alloying addition can nucleate fine, dispersed precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
A controlled heat treatment or minor alloying addition can enhance lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanoscale precipitates or enhanced lattice-distortion regions act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion through pinning and Orowan strengthening.
Increasing dislocation obstacles will increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing dislocation obstacles will increase the compressive strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
Precipitate strengthening will cause a moderate reduction in ductility without severely compromising it.
The treated alloy will contain a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates detectable by TEM or SEM.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has greater than 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C under quasi-static compression.
Excessive precipitate volume fraction or precipitate coarsening may embrittle CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed comparison is limited to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested in compression from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C at quasi-static strain rates.

contradictions.description: The boundary describes applicability to alloys processed to yield a single-phase solid solution, while the intervention and predicted outcome require formation of a detectable precipitate population, which would ordinarily make the treated material multiphase unless coherent clustering rather than a distinct phase is intended.

The hypothesis treats greater lattice distortion as a dislocation-pinning strengthening intervention, but the mechanism later describes lattice distortion as promoting ductility. The distinct roles or regimes needed to reconcile these statements are not specified.
